facts.statement: Dunkleosteus was an extinct genus of large arthrodire fish that lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 382 to 358 million years ago.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus is an extinct genus of large arthrodire ("jointed-neck") fish that existed during the Late Devonian period, about 382–358 million years ago.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus was a pelagic fish that inhabited open waters and served as one of the first vertebrate apex predators in any ecosystem.
facts.quote: It was a pelagic fish inhabiting open waters, and one of the first vertebrate apex predators of any ecosystem.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus fossils were first discovered in 1867 by Jay Terrell, an amateur paleontologist who found them in cliffs along Lake Erie near Sheffield Lake, Ohio.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus fossils were first discovered in 1867 by Jay Terrell, a hotel owner and amateur paleontologist who collected fossils in the cliffs along Lake Erie near his home of Sheffield Lake, Ohio (due west of Cleveland), United States.

facts.statement: In 1873, John Strong Newberry and the Ohio Geological Survey described the fossils donated by Jay Terrell as a single new species, Dinichthys herzeri.
facts.quote: Terrell donated his fossils to John Strong Newberry and the Ohio Geological Survey, who in 1873 described all the material as belonging to a single new genus and species: Dinichthys herzeri.

facts.statement: By 1875, further fossil discoveries revealed that multiple large fish species existed in the Ohio Shale, leading to the reclassification of the fossils.
facts.quote: However, with later fossil discoveries, by 1875 it became apparent multiple large fish species were present in the Ohio Shale.

facts.statement: Most of Jay Terrell's original fossil collection was destroyed by a fire in Elyria, Ohio, in 1873.
facts.quote: Most of Terrell's original collection does not survive, having been destroyed by a fire in Elyria, Ohio, in 1873.

facts.statement: The largest collection of Dunkleosteus fossils is at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, with smaller collections at the American Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Yale Peabody Museum, the Natural History Museum in London, and the Cincinnati Museum Center.
facts.quote: The largest collection of Dunkleosteus fossils in the world is housed at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, with smaller collections (in descending order of size) held at the American Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Yale Peabody Museum, the Natural History Museum in London, and the Cincinnati Museum Center.

facts.statement: The scientific validity of several of the ten described Dunkleosteus species remains unclear.
facts.quote: However, the validity of several of these species is unclear.

facts.statement: D. terrelli is the largest and best-known species of Dunkleosteus and serves as the type species.
facts.quote: The largest and best known species is D. terrelli, the type species.

facts.statement: Estimates for the largest known specimen of D. terrelli range from 4.1 to 10 meters in length and 1 to 4 metric tons in weight, though body shape is not fully known.
facts.quote: Since body shape is not known, various methods of estimation put the living total length of the largest known specimen of D. terrelli between 4.1 to 10 m long and its weight around 1 - 4 MT.

facts.statement: Recent studies suggest D. terrelli was likely under 5 meters long, with typical adults estimated at 3.4 meters and exceptionally large individuals reaching 4.1 meters.
facts.quote: However, current evidence suggests length of less than 5 m was more likely, with the most recent and extensive studies on the body shape and size of D. terrelli producing estimated lengths of approximately 3.4 m for typical adults and 4.1 m for exceptionally large individuals of this species.

facts.statement: Jean-Pierre Lehman named the genus Dunkleosteus in 1956 to honor David Dunkle, a former curator at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus was named by Jean-Pierre Lehman in 1956 to honour David Dunkle (1911–1984), former curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: The name Dunkleosteus combines David Dunkle's surname with the Greek word for 'bone', literally translating to 'Dunkle's bone'.
facts.quote: The genus name Dunkleosteus combines David Dunkle's surname with the Greek word ( 'bone'), literally meaning "Dunkle's bone".

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus was originally classified within the genus Dinichthys but was recognized as a distinct genus in 1956.
facts.quote: Originally thought to be a member of the genus Dinichthys, Dunkleosteus was later recognized as belonging to its own genus in 1956.

facts.statement: A 2010 phylogenetic analysis found that Dunkleosteus and Dinichthys belong to separate arthrodire clades: Dunkleosteoidea and Aspinothoracidi, respectively.
facts.quote: However, in the phylogenetic analysis of Carr and Hlavin (2010), Dunkleosteus and Dinichthys were found to belong to separate clades of arthrodires: Dunkleosteus belonged to a group called the Dunkleosteoidea while Dinichthys belonged to the distantly related Aspinothoracidi.

facts.statement: Carr and Hlavin resurrected the family Dunkleosteidae to include Dunkleosteus and Eastmanosteus along with other genera previously placed in Dinichthyidae.
facts.quote: Carr & Hlavin resurrected the family Dunkleosteidae and placed Dunkleosteus, Eastmanosteus, and a few other genera from Dinichthyidae within it.

facts.statement: Scientists have described at least ten different species of Dunkleosteus.
facts.quote: At least ten different species of Dunkleosteus have been described so far.

facts.statement: The genus Dunkleosteus is currently defined as a wastebasket taxon containing large, evolutionarily derived dunkleosteoid arthrodires.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus as currently defined is a wastebasket taxon for large dunkleosteoid arthrodires that are more evolutionarily derived than Eastmanosteus.

facts.statement: D. terrelli is the type species and is considered the largest and best-known species of Dunkleosteus.
facts.quote: The type species, D. terrelli, is the largest, best-known species of the genus.

facts.statement: Size estimates for D. terrelli range from 4.1 to 10 meters in length, although estimates exceeding 4.5 meters are poorly supported.
facts.quote: Size estimates for this species range from 4.1 - 10 m in length, though estimates greater than 4.5 m are poorly supported.

facts.statement: Skulls of D. terrelli can reach lengths of up to 60 to 70 centimeters.
facts.quote: Skulls of this species can be up to 60 - 70 cm in length.

facts.statement: Lelièvre (1982) considered D. belgicus a doubtful name and suggested the material might actually belong to Ardennosteus.
facts.quote: Lelièvre (1982) considers this taxon a nomen dubium ("doubtful name") and suggests the material may actually pertain to Ardennosteus.

facts.statement: D. marsaisi refers to fossils found in Lower Famennian Late Devonian strata of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.
facts.quote: D. marsaisi refers to the Dunkleosteus fossils from the Lower Famennian Late Devonian strata of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

facts.statement: D. marsaisi is characterized by a narrower snout and the possible presence of a postpineal fenestra.
facts.quote: In D. marsaisi, the snout is narrower, and a postpineal fenestra may be present.

facts.statement: Many researchers and authorities consider D. marsaisi to be a synonym of D. terrelli.
facts.quote: Many researchers and authorities consider it a synonym of D. terrelli.

facts.statement: D. magnificus is a large placoderm found in the Frasnian Rhinestreet Shale of New York.
facts.quote: D. magnificus is a large placoderm from the Frasnian Rhinestreet Shale of New York.

facts.statement: D. magnificus was originally described as Dinichthys magnificus by Hussakof and Bryant in 1919 and later as Dinichthys mirabilis by Heintz in 1932.
facts.quote: It was originally described as Dinichthys magnificus by Hussakof and Bryant in 1919, then as "Dinichthys mirabilis" by Heintz in 1932.

facts.statement: D. magnificus has a skull length of 55 centimeters and an estimated total length of approximately 3 meters.
facts.quote: This species has a skull length of 55 cm and a total estimated length of approximately 3 m.

facts.statement: There is a debate regarding the genus of D. magnificus, with some researchers placing it in Dunkleosteus and others in Eastmanosteus.
facts.quote: Dunkle and Lane (1971) moved it to Dunkleosteus, whereas Dennis-Bryan (1987) considered it to belong to the genus Eastmanosteus.

facts.statement: D. amblyodoratus is known from fragmentary remains found in Late Devonian strata of the Kettle Point Formation in Ontario.
facts.quote: D. amblyodoratus is known from some fragmentary remains from Late Devonian strata of Kettle Point Formation, Ontario.

facts.statement: The name D. amblyodoratus means 'blunt spear', referring to the shape formed by the nuchal and paranuchal plates at the back of the head.
facts.quote: The species name means 'blunt spear' and refers to the way the nuchal and paranuchal plates in the back of the head form the shape of a blunted spearhead.

facts.statement: D. raveri possessed comparatively large eyes in addition to its small size.
facts.quote: Besides its small size, it had comparatively large eyes.

facts.statement: The specific name D. tuderensis refers to the Maliy Tuder River, where the holotype was found.
facts.quote: The specific name refers to the Maliy Tuder River as the holotype was found on its bank.

facts.statement: Only four species are universally agreed upon as valid: D. terrelli, D. raveri, D. tuderensis, and possibly D. amblyodoratus, which is known from limited material.
facts.quote: In total, of the ten or so species listed above only four are agreed upon as valid species of Dunkleosteus by all researchers: D. terrelli (which may or may not include Dunkleosteus material from Morocco), D. raveri, D. tuderensis, and possibly D. amblyodoratus (which is known from limited material that appears distinct but is difficult to compare with other dunkleosteids).

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus possessed dermal bone armor plates covering its skull and the front half of its trunk.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus was covered in dermal bone forming armor plates across its skull and front half of its trunk.

facts.statement: The armor on the nuchal plate at the back of the Dunkleosteus skull was over 2 to 3 inches thick.
facts.quote: This armor is often described as being over 2 – 3 in thick, but this is only across the thickened nuchal plate at the back of the skull.

facts.statement: The armor on the rest of the Dunkleosteus body was generally 0.33 to 1 inch thick.
facts.quote: Across the rest of the body the armor is generally much thinner, only about 0.33 – 1 in in thickness.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus armor plates contained both a hard cortical layer and a marrow-filled cancellous layer, resembling tetrapod bones rather than teleost fish bones.
facts.quote: The plates of Dunkleosteus had both a hard cortical and a marrow-filled cancellous layer, unlike most teleost fishes and more similar to tetrapod bones.

facts.statement: Most fossilized specimens of Dunkleosteus preserve only the armored frontal sections, leaving the appearance of the rest of the fish largely unknown.
facts.quote: Mainly the armored frontal sections of specimens have been fossilized, and consequently, the appearance of the other portions of the fish is mostly unknown.

facts.statement: Only about 5% of Dunkleosteus specimens preserve more than a quarter of their skeleton.
facts.quote: In fact, only about 5% of Dunkleosteus specimens have more than a quarter of their skeleton preserved.

facts.statement: It is debated whether lengths of 5 meters or more for Dunkleosteus terrelli are accurate, as most such estimates lack quantitative or statistical backing.
facts.quote: However, most cited length estimates are speculative and lack quantitative or statistical backing, and lengths of 5 m or more are poorly supported.

facts.statement: Extensive analyses suggest typical adult Dunkleosteus terrelli were about 3.4 meters long, with rare individuals potentially reaching 4.1 meters.
facts.quote: The most extensive analyses of body size and shape in Dunkleosteus terrelli produce length estimates of ~3.4 m for typical adults of this species, with very rare and exceptional individuals potentially reaching lengths of 4.1 m.

facts.statement: A 4.6-meter-long adult Dunkleosteus terrelli was estimated to weigh 665 kilograms based on a shark-like body plan.
facts.quote: Carr (2010) estimated a 4.6 m long adult individual of Dunkleosteus terrelli to have weighed 665 kg, assuming a shark-like body plan and a similar length-weight relationship.

facts.statement: Using an ellipsoid volumetric method, a typical 3.41-meter-long adult Dunkleosteus was estimated to weigh 950 to 1200 kilograms, while the largest 4.1-meter individual weighed 1494 to 1764 kilograms.
facts.quote: Engelman (2023), using an ellipsoid volumetric method, estimated weights of 950 – 1200 kg for typical (3.41 m long) adult Dunkleosteus, and weights of 1494 – 1764 kg for the largest (4.1 m in this study) individual.

facts.statement: An exceptionally preserved specimen of Dunkleosteus terrelli shows a pectoral fin with ceratotrichia, indicating that placoderm fin morphology was more variable and influenced by locomotion than previously thought.
facts.quote: An exceptionally preserved specimen of D. terrelli preserves a pectoral fin outline with ceratotrichia, implying that the fin morphology of placoderms was much more variable than previously thought, and was heavily influenced by locomotory requirements.

facts.statement: A 2017 study reconstructed the caudal fin of Dunkleosteus terrelli with a strong ventral lobe, high aspect ratio, and narrow peduncle, differing from previous anguilliform reconstructions based on other placoderms.
facts.quote: This knowledge, coupled with the knowledge that fish morphology is more heavily influenced by feeding niche than phylogeny, allowed a 2017 study to infer the caudal fin shape of D. terrelli, reconstructing this fin with a strong ventral lobe, a high aspect ratio, narrow caudal peduncle, in contrast to previous reconstructions based on the anguilliform caudal fin of coccosteomorph placoderms.

facts.statement: The only known vertebral remains of Dunkleosteus consist of 16 vertebrae found within the trunk armor of specimen CMNH 50322.
facts.quote: The only vertebral remains known for Dunkleosteus are a small series of 16 vertebrae within the trunk armor of the specimen CMNH 50322.

facts.statement: The pelvic girdle of Dunkleosteus was relatively small compared to the overall size of its armor.
facts.quote: The pelvic girdle of Dunkleosteus is relatively small relative to the overall size of the armor.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus lived during the Late Devonian period, approximately 380 to 360 million years ago, in the Frasnian and Famennian stages.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus (de Dunkle, apellido de David Dunkle, y griego antiguo: osteos «hueso») es un género de peces placodermos artródiros que existieron a finales del período Devónico, desde hace aproximadamente 380 hasta 360 millones de años, en el Frasniense y Fameniense.

facts.statement: Fossils of some described species have been found in North America, Poland, Belgium, and Morocco.
facts.quote: De algunas especies descritas se han hallado numerosos fósiles en Norteamérica, Polonia, Bélgica y Marruecos.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus was characterized by an armored head and jaws equipped with unusual blade-like teeth.
facts.quote: Como otros diníctidos, Dunkleosteus se caracterizaba por una cabeza acorazada provista de mandíbulas con cuchillas dentales poco usuales.

facts.statement: Reaching up to six meters in length and one ton in weight, Dunkleosteus was an apex predator that likely preyed on all kinds of fauna.
facts.quote: Con hasta seis metros de largo y 1 tonelada de peso, este cazador estuvo en la cima de la cadena alimentaria de su ambiente y, probablemente, depredaba toda clase de fauna.

facts.statement: The genus Dunkleosteus was described by Lehman in 1956.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Lehman, 1956

facts.statement: The type species Dunkleosteus terrelli was originally described by Newberry in 1873.
facts.quote: type_species_authority: Newberry, 1873

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus is classified as a member of the class Placodermi, order Arthrodira, suborder Brachythoraci, family Dunkleosteidae, and superfamily Dunkleosteoidea.
facts.quote: classis: Placodermi† ordo: Arthrodira† subordo: Brachythoraci† unranked_familia: Pachyosteomorphi† superfamilia: Dunkleosteoidea† familia: Dunkleosteidae† genus: Dunkleosteus†

facts.statement: Biomechanical modeling suggests Dunkleosteus could open its jaws in 20 milliseconds and complete the process in 50 to 60 milliseconds.
facts.quote: Based on biomechanical modelling, Anderson and Westneat suggested that this mechanism allowed D. terrelli to both achieve a high speed of jaw opening, opening their jaws in 20 milliseconds and completing the whole process in 50–60 milliseconds

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the pressures generated by Dunkleosteus's bite were sufficient to puncture or cut dermal armor, indicating it preyed on armored free-swimming organisms like ammonites and other placoderms.
facts.quote: They further claimed that pressures generated in those regions were high enough to puncture or cut through cuticle or dermal armor, suggesting that D. terrelli was adapted to prey on free-swimming, armored prey such as ammonites and other placoderms.

facts.statement: In 2025, Engelman and colleagues challenged the suction feeding hypothesis, arguing that the underlying models did not accurately reflect Dunkleosteus anatomy.
facts.quote: In 2025, Engelman and colleagues questioned the suction feeding hypothesis, criticizing that the assumptions behind these models do not accurately reflect the anatomy of D. terrelli.

facts.statement: Engelman et al. (2025) suggested that Dunkleosteus had more cartilage in its skull than previously thought, allowing a jaw gape angle of at least 65 to 70 degrees.
facts.quote: Engelman et al. (2025) also suggested that the skull of Dunkleosteus was composed of more cartilage than previously assumed, including most major jaw connections and muscle attachment sites which would have allowed to widely open its jaws with a gape angle of at least 65–70°

facts.statement: Teeth of a chondrichthyan possibly belonging to Orodus were found with Dunkleosteus remains, suggesting they were regurgitated stomach contents.
facts.quote: The teeth of a chondrichthyan thought to belong to Orodus (Orodus spp.) were found in association with Dunkleosteus remains, suggesting that these were probably stomach contents regurgitated from the animal.

facts.statement: Fossils of Dunkleosteus often contain semi-digested fish bones, indicating it may have routinely regurgitated prey bones instead of digesting them.
facts.quote: Fossils of Dunkleosteus are frequently found with boluses of fish bones, semi-digested and partially eaten remains of other fish. As a result, the fossil record indicates it may have routinely regurgitated prey bones rather than digest them.

facts.statement: Mature Dunkleosteus likely inhabited deep sea locations, while juveniles lived in shallow waters.
facts.quote: Mature individuals probably inhabited deep sea locations, like other placoderms, living in shallow waters during adolescence.

facts.statement: A specimen of Dunkleosteus (CMNH 5302) and a Titanichthys (CMNH 9889) show damage attributed to puncture wounds from the bony fangs of other Dunkleosteus.
facts.quote: a specimen of Dunkleosteus (CMNH 5302), and Titanichthys (CMNH 9889), show damage said to be puncture damage from the bony fangs of other Dunkleosteus.

facts.statement: Studies show that juvenile Dunkleosteus had lower jaws proportionally as robust as adults, indicating they could produce high bite forces and shear resistant prey tissue from a young age.
facts.quote: Morphological studies on the lower jaws of juveniles of D. terrelli reveal they were proportionally as robust as those of adults, indicating they already could produce high bite forces and likely were able to shear into resistant prey tissue similar to adults, albeit on a smaller scale.

facts.statement: Evidence from other placoderms suggests some may have been viviparous, including findings of what appears to be an umbilical cord.
facts.quote: Some other placoderms have been found with evidence that they may have been viviparous, including what appears to have been an umbilical cord.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus species were estimated to be between four and six meters long and weigh approximately one ton.
facts.quote: Se estima que D. terrelli y Dunkleosteus sp. medían más o menos entre cuatro y seis metros de longitud, pesando aproximadamente 1 tonelada.

facts.statement: The skull and part of the thorax were covered by articulating bony plates forming armor, while the rest of the body was naked and scaly.
facts.quote: El cráneo y parte del tórax estaban recubiertos por placas óseas que se articulaban formando una "armadura", pero el resto del cuerpo era desnudo y escamoso.

facts.statement: Its jaws lacked true teeth and instead possessed a set of dental blades capable of tearing flesh and crushing bones.
facts.quote: Las mandíbulas carecían de dientes verdaderos y estaban dotadas de un juego de cuchillas dentales, con las que podía despedazar carne y triturar huesos.

facts.statement: The skull and thoracic shield measured 1.3 meters at their widest point, while the armor plates were 5 centimeters thick.
facts.quote: El cráneo, más el escudo torácico, medía 1,3 metros a su punto más amplio, y las placas de su armadura 5cm de grosor.

facts.statement: Its nasal capsules were not fused to the rest of the cranial vault, a feature distinguishing placoderms from other jawed vertebrates.
facts.quote: Sus cápsulas nasales no estuvieron fusionadas al resto de la bóveda craneal, algo que distingue a los placodermos de los demás vertebrados con mandíbulas.

facts.statement: The superficial tissue of the dermal bones was not dentine like most fish, but a unique placoderm tissue known as semidentine.
facts.quote: El típico tejido superficial de los huesos dérmicos (placas óseas) de Dunkleosteus no era dentina, como en la mayoría de los peces, sino un tejido único de los placodermos, conocido como semidentina.

facts.statement: The first remains of Dunkleosteus were discovered by geologist Jay Terrell in 1867 along the shores of Lake Erie in Sheffield Lake, Ohio.
facts.quote: Los primeros restos de Dunkleosteus fueron descubiertos por el geólogo Jay Terrell en 1867, a las orillas del lago Erie, en Sheffield Lake (Ohio).

facts.statement: The initial discovery consisted of a partial skull and a dorsal plate from the thoracic shield, which were later destroyed in an Elyria fire.
facts.quote: Constaban de un cráneo parcial y una placa dorsal del escudo torácico, posteriormente destruidos en un incendio de Elyria.

facts.statement: John Strong Newberry named the animal Dinichthys terrelli in 1873 in honor of its discoverer.
facts.quote: John Strong Newberry les dio el nombre de Dinichthys terrelli en 1873, en honor a su descubridor.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus belongs to the family Dinichthyidae, which was named based on the genus Dinichthys.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus pertenece a la familia Dinichthyidae, la cual se nombró con base al Dinichthys.

facts.statement: The family currently contains eleven valid genera and one doubtful one, with Dunkleosteus being the largest and most popular.
facts.quote: Actualmente, la familia contiene once géneros válidos y uno dudoso, siendo Dunkleosteus, el más grande y popular de todos.

facts.statement: No fossil material has been found for the rest of the body, indicating its vertebrae were cartilaginous or poorly ossified, explaining its fragility for fossilization, analogous to sharks.
facts.quote: Del resto del cuerpo no se ha descubierto material fósil, lo que indica que sus vértebras fueron cartilaginosas o muy poco osificadas, explicando su fragilidad para la fosilización, análogo de los tiburones.

facts.statement: Like all arthrodires, Dunkleosteus had an epaxial articulation between the dorsal plates and the skull, allowing it to raise its head upward to easily hunt large prey.
facts.quote: Al igual que todos los artrodiros, Dunkleosteus tuvo una articulación que se ubicaba entre las placas dorsales y el cráneo, conocida como epaxial, que le hubiera permitido alzar la cabeza hacia arriba, y por tanto cazar grandes presas con facilidad.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the genus Dinichthys is truly a synonym of Dunkleosteus until a re-investigation of its scarce holotype is conducted.
facts.quote: mientras no se haga una re-investigación de su escaso holotipo, no se podrá determinar si efectivamente es sinónimo o no de Dunkleosteus, como mucho se especula.

facts.statement: D. terrelli is the largest and best-known species of the genus and had a rounded snout.
facts.quote: D. terrelli Esta es la especie de mayor tamaño y mejor conocida del género. Tenía un hocico redondeado.

facts.statement: D. marsaisi refers to Dunkleosteus fossils found in Lower Famennian strata of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.
facts.quote: D. marsaisi se refiere a los fósiles de Dunkleosteus hallados en estratos de finales del Devónico del Famenniano Inferior de los Montes Atlas en Marruecos.

facts.statement: D. marsaisi has a narrower snout and may possess a postpineal fenestra.
facts.quote: En D. marsaisi, el hocico es más estrecho, y puede poseer una fenestra postpineal.

facts.statement: Many researchers consider D. marsaisi a synonym of D. terrelli, while H. Schultze considers it a member of Eastmanosteus.
facts.quote: Muchos investigadores lo consideran un sinónimo de D. terrelli. H. Schultze considera a D. marsaisi como miembro de Eastmanosteus.

facts.statement: D. magnificus was originally described as Dinichthys magnificus in 1919, renamed Dinichthys mirabilis in 1932, and transferred to Dunkleosteus in 1971.
facts.quote: Fue descrito originalmente como Dinichthys magnificus por Hussakof y Bryant en 1919, y luego como Dinichthys mirabilis por Heintz en 1932. Dunkle y Lane lo trasladaron a Dunkleosteus en 1971.

facts.statement: D. newberryi is known mainly from a 28-centimeter-long infragnathal plate with a prominent anterior cusp.
facts.quote: D. newberryi Conocido principalmente de una placa infragnatal de 28 centímetros de largo que tiene una prominente cúspide anterior.

facts.statement: The species name means "blunt spear" and refers to how the nuchal and paranuchal plates create a pointed lance-head appearance.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie significa "lanza roma" y se refiere a la forma en que las placas nucal y paranucal en la parte posterior de la cabeza crean una apariencia de cabeza de lanza despuntada.

facts.statement: Although known only from fragments, D. amblyodoratus is estimated to have reached about six meters in length.
facts.quote: Aunque solo se conoce de estos fragmentos, se estima que habría medido cerca de seis metros de largo en vida.

facts.statement: D. raveri is a small species, possibly one meter long, known from an uncrushed cranial vault found in a carbonate concretion in the Huron Shale of Ohio.
facts.quote: D. raveri es una pequeña especie, posiblemente de un metro de longitud conocida a partir de una bóveda cranueal sin aplastamiento, hallada en una concreción de carbonato hallada en el fondo del Esquisto Huron, en los estratos del Fameniano de Ohio.

facts.statement: Because D. raveri was found in strata directly below those of D. terrelli, it has been suggested that D. raveri may have given rise to D. terrelli.
facts.quote: Debido a que D. raveri fue hallado en estratos directamente por debajo de donde se hallaron los restos de D. terrelli, se ha sugerido que D. raveri pudo haber dado origen a D. terrelli.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus lived for approximately 20 million years, from the Late Givetian to Late Famennian of the Upper Devonian.
facts.quote: Los estratos que han preservado al Dunkleosteus datan del Devónico Superior, del Frasniense tardío al Fameniense tardío, por lo que existió durante aproximadamente 20 millones de años.

facts.statement: Some skull and thoracic shield fossils show cannibalistic tendencies, evidenced by bite marks matching its own dentition that did not heal.
facts.quote: Algunos fósiles del cráneo y escudo torácico demuestran que Dunkleosteus presentaba tendencias caníbales, ya que presentan mordidas que coinciden con su misma "dentadura" y que posteriormente no se curaron.

facts.statement: Calculations indicate the front blades of Dunkleosteus bit with a pressure of 5363 newtons, while the lateral blades exerted 4414 newtons.
facts.quote: Los cálculos indican que las cuchillas frontales mordían a una presión de 5363 newtons, mientras las laterales a una de 4414.

facts.statement: While earlier studies speculated the bite was strong but slow, research showed the skull's multiple joints allowed for an extremely rapid bite.
facts.quote: Anteriores investigaciones especularon que la mordida era fuerte pero lenta, sin embargo este mismo estudio demostró que el cráneo, al poseer varias articulaciones, adquirió también una mordida extremadamente rápida.

facts.statement: The most common Dunkleosteus fossils are armor plates, often from juveniles or semi-adults, which have allowed growth studies.
facts.quote: Los fósiles más comunes de Dunkleosteus son las placas de su armadura, y muchas de estas suelen provenir de individuos juveniles o semi-adultos, algo que ha permitido análisis y estudios sobre su crecimiento.

facts.statement: Dunkleosteus coexisted with sharks, acanthodians, arthropods, mollusks, and other placoderms, which it hunted.
facts.quote: Dunkleosteus coexistió con tiburones, acantodios, artrópodos, moluscos y otros placodermos, a los cuales cazaba.

facts.statement: This predator likely occupied the top of its ecosystem's food chain, earning the title of superpredator.
facts.quote: Es muy probable que este depredador se encontrase en la cima de la cadena trófica de su ecosistema, pasando a ser denominado superpredador.

facts.statement: Fossils in Europe and Morocco show Dunkleosteus had a much wider distribution, traveling across Euramerica and reaching Gondwana's coasts.
facts.quote: Aunque las poblaciones de Dunkleosteus abundaban en estos ecosistemas, los hallazgos en Europa y Marruecos demuestran que su distribución fue, en general, mucho mayor, y que debió recorrer todo el continente de Euramérica, llegando incluso a las costas de Gondwana.
